title: Start With What Grows Near You
body:
Occult botany is not about rare herbs from far away; it is about the plants in your own hedgerow, garden or windowbox, and the long folk record of how people used them. Beginners who start local learn faster, because they can observe the plant through a whole year rather than reading about it.

The book is built around that principle: identify, observe, then work — never the other way round.

title: Folklore Is Data, Not Decoration
body:
Plant lore survives because it encoded something useful — timing, danger, medicinal effect, seasonal signal. Treating it as quaint misses the point; treating it as literal is worse. The green practitioner's skill is reading the folklore for what it remembers.

Rosemary for remembrance is a poem. Rosemary as a preservative and a stimulant is why the poem exists.

title: Safety Before Mystique
body:
Any honest guide to magical herbs has to say plainly which plants will hurt you. Foxglove, monkshood, hemlock — beautiful, storied, and lethal — appear in most old herbals, and a modern beginner's book that romanticises them is negligent.

Occult Botany for Beginners keeps the poisons in a separate chapter with clear warnings. Respect for the plant includes knowing when to leave it alone.
